The fifth meeting of the Disarmament and International Security Committee, First Committee of the 80th session of the General Assembly is called to order. Distinguished delegates, the Committee will continue this afternoon with its general debate on all disarmament and international security agenda items allocated to it. I do count on your cooperation to respect the time limit for statements and to speak at a reasonable speed to allow adequate interpretation. Longer statements can be shared to e-statements to be posted on the UN journal. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ukraine on behalf of a group of states.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. I have the honor to speak on behalf of Albania, Andorra, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, Montenegro, the Netherlands, New Zealand, North Macedonia, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Republic of Korea, Republic of Moldova, Romania, San Marino, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and my own country, Ukraine. We reaffirm our firm commitment to the rules-based international order founded on the UN Charter and fundamental principles of international law. Russia's ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine represents a blatant violation of international law and a direct threat to global peace and security, undermining efforts to uphold non-proliferation and disarmament stipulated by the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. Russia's actions endanger global food security, energy stability, nuclear safety and security, and the environment, disproportionately affecting the most vulnerable populations worldwide. We condemn in the strongest possible terms Russia's aggressive actions and irresponsible and nuclear rhetoric in its illegal, unjustified and unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine. We express our serious concern with Russia's most recent airspace violations in Estonia, Poland and Romania, which are unacceptable, escalatory and irresponsibly undermining international security. We strongly condemn Russia's continued indiscriminate attacks killing civilians and destroying civilian objects, including critical energy infrastructure. Especially regarding the approaching winter, the energy security of Ukraine is seriously undermined by Russia. We express serious concern that the situation at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant remains precarious, with six of the seven indispensable pillars for nuclear safety and security of the Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency being compromised fully or partially. We are also deeply concerned by the nuclear safety and security risks posed by the vulnerabilities in Ukraine's electricity grid resulting from Russia's attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. This includes the disconnection of Ukraine's ZNPP. from its last external power supply since 23rd September which poses significant challenges for nuclear safety we also note with concern the damage arising from the 14th February 2025 drone strike against the new safe confinement at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant built with International effort to ensure nuclear safety we firmly reject any attempts to consider the restart of the reactors at Ukraine's znpb which would be inconsistent with well-established nuclear safety principles. Any restart of the reactors at the ZNPP can only take place once the facility has been returned to the legitimate control and oversight of Ukraine's competent regulatory authority. We support the continued physical presence of IAEA experts at Ukraine's ZNPP in full respect of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine. The safety and security of the agency staff remain of paramount importance. Delays in the completion of the IAEA's support and assistance mission to Zaporizhzhia rotations are unacceptable and we call on the Russian Federation to immediately cease any actions which hinder the timely conduct of ISAM's rotations and put the safety of the agency staff at risk. We urge Russia to immediately cease all hostile actions against Ukrainian nuclear facilities and to withdraw its military and associated personnel from Ukraine's NPP without delay, as required by the resolutions of the IAEA General Conference and Board of Governors, as well as the UN General Assembly. Moreover, the release of the unlawfully detained Ukrainian ZNPP personnel by the occupying Russian authorities remains not only a humanitarian imperative, it is a precondition for restoring basic trust and operational safety at the site. We are seriously concerned by reports of the use of riot control agents by Russia as a method of warfare, as well as the alleged use of choking agent chloropicrin against Ukrainian servicemen. In this regard, we note the findings of the technical secretariat of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons reports of 18 November 2024, 14 February 2025, and 20 June 2025 concerning the OPCW technical assistant visits requested by Ukraine, which confirm the presence of riot control agents in samples taken from the front lines in the Dnipro Petrovsk region of Ukraine. We stress that any use of riot control agents as a method of warfare or chloropicrin constitute a violation of the Chemical Weapons Convention and the global norm against the use of chemical weapons and must be stopped immediately. Mr. Chair, we strongly condemn the continued military support provided to Russia by Belarus, Iran, and the DPRK, which enables Russia to sustain its illegal war of aggression against Ukraine. We strongly condemn the ongoing military cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including DPRK's provision of ballistic missiles, artillery shells, other military material, and the deployment of significant number of DPRK troops to Russia in combat operations against Ukraine. Such actions mark a dangerous expansion of the war with serious consequences for European and Indo-Pacific security and represent flagrant violations of multiple UN Security Council resolutions. We remain alarmed about the statements made by Russian officials claiming that the DPRK's denuclearization is off the table, which is inconsistent with Russia's NPT obligations. The DPRK cannot and will never have the status of a nuclear weapons state in accordance with the NPT. We strongly condemn the transfer of advanced weaponry by Iran to Russia, which are used in Russia's illegal war of aggression against Ukraine and in relentless attacks against the civilian population. These transfers directly contribute to Russia's escalating violence in Ukraine, further threatening European security. We urge all countries to immediately cease any direct or indirect assistance to Russia in its war of aggression against Ukraine, including the provision of direct military aid and the supply of use goods and sensitive items that sustained Russia's war effort. Mr. Chair, we reaffirm our commitment to the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders, extending to its territorial waters, as well as for Ukraine's inherent right to self-defense against the illegal Russian aggression. We remain steadfast in our commitment to ensure Russia's accountability for the serious crimes under international law committed in the Ukrainian territory and for the extensive damage caused by its actions. We welcome the joint efforts by the United States, Ukraine, Europe and others to stop the killing, to end Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine and to achieve just, comprehensive and lasting peace consistent with the Charter of the United Nations. We urge the international community to use its influence and maximize pressure on Russia to immediately end this unlawful aggression. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Ukraine for her statement on behalf of a group of states, and I give the floor to her Excellency, Permanent Representative of Australia to the United Nations Office in Geneva and to the Conference on Disarmament.

Thank you, Chair. Let me begin by welcoming the breakthrough on the first phase of the plan to bring peace to Gaza. Agreement to a ceasefire and the disarming of Hamas are of special importance to the work of this committee. We acknowledged President Trump's leadership and the role of Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey in this outcome. Chair, 80 years ago, emerging from the devastation, grief, and the ruin of war, the people of our nations came together and put their trust in each other's humanity. Since then, the UN has achieved much through collective effort to achieve global peace and security. Building a strong disarmament, non-proliferation and arms control architecture. Guarding against the spread of nuclear weapons and working for a world free of nuclear weapons. Developing norms and regulating the development, use and trade in weapons. Chair, our collective efforts here in First Committee matter. The world faces increasingly complex challenges. Russia's ongoing illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine exemplifies the extent of these challenges and the institutions we have worked arduously together to build are under strain. International peace and security needs effective multilateralism. This is not somebody else's problem. It is up to each member state to do its part. Chair, we must lift our gaze and be laser focused on what we are here to do. For Australia, this means First, fighting hard to hold on to what matters, those irreplaceable institutions and rules that we have built and which continue to make us safe. The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, the International Atomic Energy Agency, the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, and international humanitarian law. Second, complex challenges require us to be creative, innovative, and to find new ways of working. Not every problem needs a treaty. Political declarations, norms of responsible state behavior, effective export control regimes, confidence building measures, these help reinforce and support this architecture. Third, how we do our work matters, collaboration, listening, dialogue, and inclusion. We must look for modest, incremental, practical measures to move us forward. Chair, we need to stand up for what matters. The NPT is one of the great achievements of multilateralism. It has made the world safer and continues to do so. It is essential to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons and build realistic pathways to their elimination. At next year's review conference, Australia will work to preserve the ongoing security benefits of the treaty and strengthen its implementation, to address proliferation threats like that posed by Iran's nuclear program and DPRK's ongoing development of nuclear weapons in violation of multiple UN Security Council resolutions, to back the independent technical authority of the IAEA, to negotiate for more transparency, accountability and effective reporting, to agree practical measures for action to reduce the risk of nuclear conflict. Chair, the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty has created powerful global rules against nuclear testing, which have a high compliance track record and must be protected. Its international monitoring system provides an essential global public good. The Chemical Weapons Convention has helped rid the world of all declared chemical weapons, but some states are flouting its rules. We must work together to ensure that the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons can respond effectively to chemical weapons threat and use and prevent the re-emergence of stockpiles. We must also address growing biological threats, including through strengthening the Biological Weapons Convention. Chair, humanitarian disarmament treaties are under increasing pressure and states are having to grapple with difficult choices. Landmark treaties such as the anti-personnel mine ban and cluster munition conventions have helped save countless lives since entering into force. So it is regrettable that some states have decided to withdraw from these conventions. Australia will continue to reinforce their value and urge their universalization and implementation. Chair, Australia supports creative and innovative approaches to address the challenges of our times. Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence present great opportunities. They also present risks. Australia is committed to the responsible use of AI in the military domain. AI technologies must comply with international law, including IHL and international human rights law throughout their life cycle. Chair, space touches every aspect of our lives, from international communications networks to military and defense capabilities. Australia supports an approach centered on responsible behaviors that actively promote safety, predictability, and stability in the space environment. We are firmly committed to promoting peace and security in cyberspace by shaping and upholding the framework for responsible state behavior in cyberspace. Chair, Australia's commitment to bolstering the non-proliferation and disarmament regime is not rhetorical. We back our words with actions. As permanent chair of the Australia Group, which celebrated its 40th anniversary this year, we are proud to be a global leader in multilateral export control regimes that deliver vital outcomes to prevent the proliferation of chemical and biological weapons. As co-chair of the ASEAN Regional Forum's work on non-proliferation and disarmament with the Philippines and New Zealand, Australia is working with ASEAN partners to build mutual understanding and reduce the risk of conflict in the Indo-Pacific. As joint coordinator of the nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament initiatives with Philippines and Japan, we are working to build consensus at next year's NPT review conference. And as chair of the IAEA Board of Governors for 25-26, Australia is working hard to support the IAEA to deliver vital nuclear safeguards, security and safety outcome for its members. Chair, how we work together as an international community is critical to our success. Australia values listening, dialogue, inclusivity, respect. Durable peace is impossible without the full, equal and meaningful participation of diverse voices. Here at the United Nations, all voices are welcome. Limit those voices and we limit our successes. Ahead of the 25th anniversary of the landmark UN Security Council Resolution 1325, Australia is proud to champion the Women, Peace and Security agenda as a cornerstone of our foreign and defence policy. Chair, first committee gives us, the international community, five weeks to work together to make progress and protect the rules and institutions we all rely on. We all have a part to play and Australia will play its part. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia for her statement. I give now the floor to His Excellency, Permanent Representative of Ireland to the United Nations Office in Geneva.

Chairman, thank you. Firstly, congratulations on your assumption of the chair. Ireland, of course, offers you our full support. Ireland aligns, Chair, with statements of the European Union and the New Agenda Coalition. Once again, Chair, we meet amidst multiple serious crises, each of which reflects and shapes our work on disarmament, global challenges and threats to peace. Russia's unjustified and illegal full-scale invasion of Ukraine is now in its fourth year. Russia's use of nuclear rhetoric and threats, violations of international law, targeting of civilians, use of chemical weapons on the battlefield, and ongoing illegal occupation of the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant are unacceptable and reprehensible. Ireland unequivocally condemns Russia's actions. A comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law is a key priority. Ireland welcomes that Israel and Hamas have agreed on the first phase of a peace deal to end the war in Gaza and that all living hostages have been released. The peace deal offers an opportunity to address the catastrophic humanitarian situation and unconscionable human suffering in Gaza. to put an end to the man-made famine and to restore the vital medical, educational and other social services which have been decimated in Gaza over the past two years. All members of this United Nations must reflect on what more they can do. The non-proliferation challenges in Iran are profound and urgent. Iran must engage meaningfully and in good faith with the international community to satisfy concerns about its nuclear programme. The JCPOA showed that when all relevant parties are engaged, Iran's nuclear activities can be verifiably constrained. We must recommit to a lasting and sustainable diplomatic solution. This must involve Iran's full cooperation with the IAEA, including through implementing its legal obligations. Chair, through these urgent and pressing crises, we can see disturbing themes. We have seen conflicts involving nuclear armed states, continued obstruction in multilateral organizations, attacks on the integrity of international institutions, including the IAEA, flagrant breaches of international law, including international humanitarian law, violations of sovereignty and territorial integrity, and attacks on nuclear facilities. Ireland echoes the concern of the IAEA Director General at the UN Security Council on the consequences of such attacks, including for regional and global stability. Amidst this, the disarmament and non-proliferation architecture is under real strain. Upholding it and its successes is not a passive exercise. It takes real political will and effort. Over the next year, we will come together in the context of a number of review conferences. We will engage in good faith to achieve a positive, meaningful outcome at the NPT Review Conference. We are not unaware of the challenge involved, but it is crucial that we maintain the NPT as an essential element of the disarmament and non-proliferation regime. We continue to call for the balanced implementation of its three pillars, in particular disarmament, which has lagged behind. We will advance proposals for increased transparency, especially by the nuclear weapons states, to drive accountability for disarmament obligations and commitments. We welcome the establishment of the independent scientific panel to examine the effects of nuclear war, mandated by the General Assembly and proposed by Ireland and New Zealand. The panel will provide an up-to-date understanding of the consequences of these weapons, demonstrating with the latest science, scientific data, and modeling. that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. We look forward to the presentation by the chair of the panel to this committee. In its 30th anniversary, we will call for long overdue progress made more difficult still by Russia's deratification towards the effective implementation of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. We must continue to safeguard the norm against nuclear testing. We will continue to advocate for the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons as an effective means of advancing and achieving nuclear disarmament motivated by the awareness of the catastrophic humanitarian and environmental consequences of nuclear weapons, and this in full complementarity with the global disarmament and non-proliferation regime. We will support international organizations, in particular the IAEA and the OPCW, in their crucial and impartial work. We call on all states to ensure full cooperation with the work of the agency. Ireland strongly supports the OPCW in identifying, documenting, and eliminating chemical weapons in Syria. We take good note of the UN Secretary General's call for urgent progress on a legally binding instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems. We welcome the work of the group of governmental experts in the CCW. The rolling text currently being developed represents a comprehensive set of elements sufficient to form the basis of negotiations. and in that spirit we are pleased to co-sponsor with Austria and the cross-regional group a resolution on this topic. Chair, Ireland is a proud champion of the Secretary General's advocacy campaign on humanitarian disarmament and mine action. The Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention, the Convention on Cluster Munitions and the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons are key treaties that continue to save countless lives and prevent serious injury during conflict and for decades after. We call on all states parties to uphold their commitments under these conventions and we call on all those who have not yet done so to join without delay. It remains a key priority for Ireland to address the wide-ranging effects of the use of explosive weapons in populated areas. In 2024, EWEPA affected 74 countries and territories. Over 90% of casualties were civilians. Ireland encourages states that have yet to do so to endorse and implement the EWEPA political declaration. Ireland looks forward to the international conference in Costa Rica with a view to advancing best practice for civilian protections in conflict zones. We all have a stake in disarmament. The invaluable contributions of civil society, academia, and most importantly, the input and perspectives of victims and survivors of these weapons must be recognized and promoted. Chair, the achievement of gender equality is a longstanding priority for Ireland. But in terms of progress, the disarmament and non-proliferation field continues to lag in this area. Today, we are even in danger of reversing that limited progress. To achieve sustainable peace and development, the full, equal, and meaningful participation of women in all our efforts must be realized. Chairman, in conclusion, international disarmament and non-proliferation architecture provides the structure to tackle the challenges we face today. and to protect civilians from the impact of armed conflict. That architecture must be protected and it must be reinforced. Ireland reaffirms its commitment to that task and to upholding and strengthening international humanitarian law. Thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ireland for his statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Czechia.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Let me begin by congratulating you on your election as chair of the first committee. Czechia fully subscribes to the statement delivered by the European Union. Allow me to add several remarks in our national capacity. At a time of profound crisis for international peace and security, Czechia reaffirms its unwavering commitment to international law, effective arms control, disarmament, and non-proliferation. The first committee remains an essential forum for upholding these principles, fostering dialogue, and strengthening collective security. That is why we condemn Russia's deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure, including repeated strikes on Ukraine's energy grid that has caused immense suffering and heightened nuclear safety risks. Adding to that, Russia's reckless nuclear rhetoric, nuclear threats, and announced deployment of nuclear weapons to Belarus are provocative, dangerous, and destabilizing. The continued occupation of the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant with repeated outages of the plant's off-site power supply illustrates Russia's blatant disregard for nuclear safety and security. We thank the IAEA for its impartial efforts to uphold safety at the power plant and reiterate that the plant must be returned to full Ukrainian control. We also remain deeply alarmed by Russia's use of chemical agents as a method of warfare in Ukraine in flagrant violation of the Chemical Weapons Convention. Czechia expresses its appreciation to the OPCW for its indispensable work in upholding the global prohibition of the use of chemical weapons. We fully support the OPCW's ongoing efforts in Syria and hope that the new Syrian authorities will cooperate fully and transparently to ensure the complete elimination of all remaining chemical weapons and related capabilities in full compliance with the convention. Chair, the NPT remains the cornerstone of the global security architecture. Its three pillars are of equal importance, and we must ensure their balanced implementation. Czechia attaches the highest importance to the NPT. and wishes to see a constructive and forward-looking outcome of the forthcoming 11th Review Conference. We stand ready to work closely with the Chair of all States Parties to ensure the continued strength and effective implementation of the NPT. It is responsibility of all NPT nuclear weapon states to act transparently and responsibly. In this regard, we are increasingly concerned by China's opaque and rapid nuclear buildup, which is inconsistent with its declared no first use policy. We call on China to engage in meaningful arms control discussions. Likewise, we underscore the importance of the New START Treaty as a key element of global strategic stability and call on Russia to meaningfully engage with the United States in negotiations on a successor agreement that preserves and strengthens the existing arms control architecture. On Iran, the IAEA has repeatedly concluded that it cannot confirm the exclusively peaceful nature of its nuclear program. Iran must resume full cooperation with the IAEA without preconditions. Failing to meet its legal obligations stemming from its NPT safeguards agreement, Iran has left the international community no choice but to reimpose lawful UN sanctions. We call on Iran to address all concerns arising from its nuclear program and engage in good faith negotiations. Similarly, we condemn the DPRK's continued illegal nuclear and missile programs, as well as Russia's attempts to shield Pyongyang from accountability and to exploit illicit arm transfers. This is a direct violation of the relevant Security Council resolutions and a grave threat to regional and global security. We are alarmed that, in pursuit of its neo-colonialist objectives in Ukraine, Russia has repeatedly undermined the very core of the NPT by claiming support for DPRK's status as a nuclear weapons state. Chair, on emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and lethal autonomous weapon systems, we must move urgently to establish norms of responsible use and behavior. Czechia fully supports the Responsible Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain Initiative as an important forum for addressing the military uses of artificial intelligence and promoting responsible behaviors in this field. We also thank the Chair of the GGE on Laws, Ambassador of the Netherlands, for his effective leadership and continued efforts to advance discussions within the CCW framework. Similarly, we need to uphold and develop existing norms of responsible behavior in outer space, where irresponsible actions risk undermining the peaceful use of this domain. Czechia welcomes the beginning of substantive work in the open-ended working group on PAROS and regrets that Russia continues to disregard the overwhelming consensus on this issue. Mr. Chair, Czechia reiterates its strong commitment to multilateralism. This is why we cannot remain silent about the persistent deadlock of the Conference on Disarmament combined with its lack of inclusivity. This situation runs counter to the very spirit of the UN 80 process, which should strengthen, not weaken, multilateralism and inclusion. Russia bears much of the responsibility for this situation by systematically blocking numerous observers from participating in the work of the conference, which should be plainly reflected in its report. Mr. Chair, the profound deterioration of the security environment, driven above all by Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, leaves us no choice but to increase our defense spending, not out of preference, but out of necessity to protect our people and uphold peace. It is therefore not surprising that under such dire security circumstances, several states have also felt compelled to withdraw from the Ottawa Convention, forced to take such steps by Russia's aggression and persistent threats to their very existence. That said, we remain committed to working constructively with all UN members to ensure that disarmament and non-proliferation deliver real security for future generations. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
Thank you, distinguished representative of Czechia, for your statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Malaysia.

Thank you, Chair. My delegation congratulates you and the members of the Bureau on your election and assures you of our full support. Malaysia aligns itself with the statements made by NAM and ASEAN. Conflicts around the world are poignant reminders of the urgency of concrete action on disarmament and international security. In Gaza, there must be an end to the horrific death, destruction, and humanitarian catastrophe suffered by the Palestinian people. Eighty years after the establishment of the United Nations, much more needs to be done to reaffirm the faith of the global community and the sanctity of its charter and international law and the founding aspiration of the UN to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war. Malaysia remains deeply concerned over the unchecked expansion and qualitative enhancement of nuclear arsenals as well as the persistence of nuclear sharing arrangements and extended deterrence doctrines, which collectively undermine international peace and security. While possessed or relied upon by a select group, these weapons pose an existential threat to all states. Following two consecutive review conferences without substantive outcome, it is vital that we uphold the credibility and integrity of the NPT, renewed political will is required to ensure a successful NPT review conference in 2026, the universalization of the Treaty and the realization of the grand bargain upon which it is predicated. The nuclear weapons states, if full and effective implementation of their disarmament obligations and commitments cannot be indefinitely deferred and should be supported by increased transparency and accountability. Malaysia welcomes the steady advancement of the TPNW, which reflects the moral, security and humanitarian imperative of the total elimination of nuclear weapons. We will maintain an active role in the Treaty's intersessional work ahead of the first review conference next year. At the same time, other components of the nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation architecture must be strengthened. Malaysia reiterates its call on the remaining Annex II States to sign and ratify the CTBT without delay or preconditions. We also call for the resumption of the implementation of the New START Treaty and the negotiation of a successor agreement by its parties. This is essential in preserving arms control gains and implementing Article VI of the NPT. Malaysia fully supports efforts to strengthen existing nuclear weapon free zones and to establish new zones, including in the Middle East. As ASEAN chair during the current session of the first committee, Malaysia will coordinate the tabling of the biennial resolution on the Southeast Asia Nuclear Weapon Free Zone, SEANWFZ or Bangkok Treaty. We remain committed to continuously engaging all nuclear weapon states, including those with reservations, and to intensifying the efforts of all parties to resolve all outstanding issues in accordance with the objectives and principles of the Chonfess Treaty. In addition, Malaysia will present our annual first committee resolution on follow up to the advisory opinion of the ICJ on the legality of the threat or use of nuclear weapons, which remains of contemporary relevance. Malaysia reiterates its firm commitment to the CWC, including as a current member of the Executive Council of the OPCW. We will also continue to advance the objectives of the BWC by strengthening national implementation measures in accordance with Article IV and supporting the constructive discussions under the Working Group on Strengthening the Convention, particularly on effective verification. Chair, it is important that multilateral discourse on security issues proceeds in an inclusive manner, avoiding fragmentation and duplication, and facilitating the effective participation of developing countries. In this connection, my delegation is pleased with progress made under the OEWG on the prevention of an arms race in outer space pursuant to GA decision 79/512. Outer space must be protected in the common interest of all states, and be used exclusively for peaceful purposes. We also welcome the adoption of the final report of the OEWG on ICT security 2021 to 2025 and look forward to the operationalization of the new global mechanism. Further, my delegation recognizes the need for sustained dialogue on, inter alia, lethal autonomous weapon systems and the impact of artificial intelligence in the military domain with effective human control and compliance with international law as key considerations. Chair, in his recent report, the UN Secretary General noted the prevailing cycle of escalating military investment that stifles human development and feeds systemic instability. This underlines the indispensable role of the First Committee and the UN disarmament machinery more broadly especially in times of heightened major power rivalry and geopolitical tension. Let us work together in navigating the challenges at hand, guided by the enduring value of multilateral cooperation, the principles of the UN Charter and international law. I thank you, Chair.
Thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia for his statement. I give now the floor to her Excellency, Permanent Representative of Cabo Verde.

Thank you, Mr. Chairperson. Since this is the first time we are taking the floor, we would like to congratulate you and the members of the Bureau on your election to lead the work of the first Commission. We also express deep appreciation for the work carried out by the previous Chair and her team. You can count on Cabo Verde's continuous support. We align ourselves with the statements by the non-aligned movement and the African group and add the following in national capacity. Cabo Verde, a peaceful island state committed to multilateralism, welcomes the opportunity to participate in this discussion on disarmament and international security. Although we do not possess nuclear weapons, Cabo Verde ratified all major international disarmament instruments, reaffirming our commitment to peace, collective security, and the primacy of international law. We live in peace, but we are not immune to the cross-cutting impacts of global insecurity. Armed conflict, weapons proliferation, and the absence of clear norms directly affect human security, sustainable development and regional stability. The continued existence of nuclear arsenals poses an existential threat to humanity. The instability they generate undermine collective security and diverts resources that could be applied in the SDGs and save millions of lives. Total elimination of nuclear weapons is a collective responsibility and a moral imperative. Durable security can only be achieved through the permanent removal of these weapons from the international landscape. We therefore call for the universalization of the TPNW, the revitalization of the NPT, with renewed focus on Article 6 and the ratification of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, CMTBT, by the remaining states. Peace is not merely absence of war, but also the absence of existential threats. We strongly condemn the use of threat and use of chemical and biological weapons. Seats, with limited resources are particularly vulnerable to the cross-border impacts of incidents involving such weapons. We advocate for strengthening verification mechanisms under the Chemical Weapons Convention and enhancing international cooperation for technical capacity building, especially in developing countries. Effective prevention requires robust norms and international solidarity to ensure that all states have adequate response capabilities. The security of some states cannot be built upon the vulnerability of others. Accountability and transparency in conventional weapons production and trade are essential and we urge industrial capacity states to assume greater responsibility in export regulation, especially small arms, whose proliferation fuel conflicts beyond borders and undermine development efforts. There's a need for regional platforms with UN technical support for tracking and destroying obsolete stockpiles. Tabouert advocates that outer space remains a common good of humanity, free from militarization that would pose systemic threats to global peace and civilian infrastructure. Space must be preserved as a domain of scientific cooperation and collective progress, not transformed into a new arena of geopolitical confrontation. It is time to negotiate a legally binding instrument prohibiting the placement of weapons in space and ensuring the peaceful and equitable use of space technologies. Digital security is another integral part of international security. Digital trust is a pillar of international stability. Cyber attacks and digital misinformation have disproportionate impact on the most vulnerable states. The global digital compact and the work of the open ending working group on ICTs have our total support. The role of UN regional centers for peace and disarmament and the creation of a South Atlantic forum for sustainable security with UN support and participation of coastal states are vital. Regional capacity building in the South Atlantic and elsewhere is essential to ensure that all states can fully participate in multilateral disarmament and security processes. Regional peace is built through inclusion, cooperation and mutual respect. To strengthen multilateral disarmament mechanisms and international security, we need to assure inclusiveness and full participation. This is not only a matter of fairness, but a necessary condition for the effectiveness and legitimacy of multilateral decisions. Mr. Chair, Cabo Verde reaffirms its commitments to peace, disarmament and the strengthening of the multilateral system and stands ready to work with you, your team and all member states and partners. We are better together. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cabo Verde for her statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Nepal.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. At the outset, let me congratulate you and the members of the Bureau on your election. I assure you of my delegation's full support and cooperation in discharging your responsibilities. Nepal aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uganda on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. Mr. Chair, the world is witnessing the highest number of conflicts since World War II. The architecture of global peace and disarmament has come under severe pressure. To our utmost dismay, the defense budget is skyrocketing, reaching USD 2.7 trillion in 2024, while development cooperation is declining. And above all, the specter of nuclear war still haunts us. This year marks 80 years since the first use of nuclear weapons and 55 years since the entry into force of the landmark treaty on non-proliferation of nuclear weapons. These anniversaries underscore the urgency of our renewed commitment to disarmament and multilateral cooperation. At it is distressing that we are backtracking on many fronts of nuclear disarmament. Trust among nations has eroded. States are increasingly inclined towards policies such as nuclear deterrence and nuclear sharing. The prominence of nuclear weapons in military doctrines remains undiminished. The modernization of nuclear capabilities, including the potential integration of artificial intelligence, has posed new challenges. These developments threaten to undermine decades of progress towards a world free of nuclear weapons. Mr. Chair, it is our strong belief that total elimination of nuclear weapons is the only guarantee against the use or threat of such horrendous weapons. Nepal unequivocally calls for the general and complete disarmament of nuclear weapons in a time-bound manner. We also call for a robust verification mechanism to ensure that all parties adhere to the agreed terms, considering the interrelated and mutually reinforcing nature of the three pillars of the NPT. In this regard, we look forward to a successful convening of the 11th Review Conference of the NPT slated for next year under the presidency of Vietnam. As the cornerstone of the global nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime, we urge the universalization of the NPT. Nepal underscores the urgent resumption of negotiations on a fissile material cut-off treaty to further strengthen nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regimes. We express our full support for the establishment of nuclear weapons-free zones in all regions. We support the inalienable rights of all states, as enshrined in Article IV of the NPT, to develop and utilize nuclear technology for peaceful purposes. The IAEA should continue to promote the peaceful uses of nuclear energy while further strengthening its safeguards mechanisms to prevent proliferation. We call for legally binding security assurances to non-nuclear weapon states against the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons under any circumstances. As a party to the Chemical Weapons Convention, Nepal calls on all to comply fully with the Convention and its verification regime. This year, as we mark the 50th anniversary of the enforcement of the Biological Weapons Convention, we must ensure that the treaty is enforced effectively to prevent the misuse of biology and respond effectively to emerging biological risk. The illicit trade in small arms and light weapons must be effectively controlled to prevent conflict, reduce violence, and promote sustainable peace. As emerging and dual-use technologies are posing new challenges to disarmament, it is essential to strengthen inclusive global governance that guarantees human oversight, ensures responsible, well-regulated, and ethical use of AI technologies, fosters stronger international cooperation, and supports capacity building in developing nations. It is critical to regulate lethal autonomous weapon systems by considering their ethical, legal, humanitarian, and technological aspects. Mr. Chair, the advent of space-based weapons and anti-satellite systems represents a new frontier in arms control, underscoring the need for innovative approaches to disarmament. Outer space must be spared from the perils of arms race and weaponization of any kind while utilizing it exclusively for peaceful purposes. We call for enhanced transparency and confidence building measures in all activities related to outer space. Nepal underscores the importance of establishing a global regulatory framework to ensure an open, secure and accessible information and communication technology environment and cyberspace. Mr. Chair, the disarmament machinery such as UN Disarmament Commission and the Conference on Disarmament needs to be further extended to deliver on their mandates. Nepal supports incorporating gender perspectives into disarmament frameworks, recognizing the catalytic roles that women, youth, and civil society actors can play within the disarmament architecture. The regional disarmament architecture complements the global disarmament framework by fostering understanding, dialogue and confidence building measures. As in the past years, Nepal will table a draft resolution entitled United Nations Regional Center for Peace and Disarmament in Asia and the Pacific in our capacity as the host state. We look forward to receiving the continued support of all member states for the adoption of this resolution by consensus. In conclusion, Mr. Chair, disarmament is not merely about abolishing weapons. It is about saving lives. A fraction of global military spending could fund the UN's sustainable development goals, including eradicating extreme poverty and hunger. I appeal to the international community to pursue disarmament in action together. Only then can we build a safe, peaceful and prosperous world for all. I thank you.
Thank the distinguished representative of Nepal for his statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Kyrgyzstan.

Mr. Chair, let me also congratulate you on your election as the chair of first committee. You have the full support of my delegation during your chairmanship. I also congratulate the members of bureau on their elections. Mr. Chair, Kyrgyzstan reaffirms its commitment to international law and UN charter. We fully support the UN's efforts to maintain peace and security. Today's complex global realities test the UN's strength and effectiveness as a universal decision-making body. An effective first committee focused on security and disarmament will promote global peace and stability. As the president of the Kyrgyz Republic, His Excellency Sadyr Japarov mentioned at the GA, we face the stark paradox. More than three trillion US dollar is spent on weapons every year, while millions of people lack access to water, healthcare and education. We call to redirecting this resource to improve lives and hunger, protect the environment and to clean our air. Military spending in conflicts harm many countries. This increases poverty and inequality. We must shift resources from war to solving global challenges, climate change, displacement, and building future generations. Investing in people, education, and sustainability, not weapons, is the path to peace. We must rethink global security priorities. True security means cooperation, understanding, and trust. Ladies and gentlemen, recent developments in Central Asia highlight positive examples of states peacefully addressing longstanding border disputes. Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan demonstrated political will and diplomatic maturity by engaging in peaceful dialogue and signing agreements on border delimitation. These efforts represent a significant contribution to regional peace and set a strong precedent for other regions facing similar challenges. Continuing the discussions on borders, I am pleased to announce the new resolution. Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan will submit a new resolution entitled Support for the Peaceful Settlement of Border Disputes under agenda item prevention of armed conflict. We count on the support of the member states this important and timely initiative. Kyrgyzstan as a candidate for the non-permanent member to the Security Council for 27, 28, and as a country that has never been elected to the Security Council, is ready to contribute to the efforts on maintaining peace. Mr. Chair, let me once again reiterate our support for the global efforts for the nuclear weapon free world. Their total elimination is only guaranteed against use and threat. During the high level week, Last month, Kyrgyzstan signed the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, TPNW. This shows our strong commitment to nuclear disarmament, non-proliferation, and global security. Our accession reflects Kyrgyzstan's consistent support for the nuclear weapon free world. Kyrgyzstan has ratified the additional protocol to the IAEA safeguards agreement. and together with the NPT is another testament to our transparency and readiness to cooperate. We firmly believe that the CTBT's early entry into the force is vital for strengthening the global non-proliferation and disarmament regime. We also highlight the key role of the NPT as a foundation of the nuclear disarmament. Ahead of the 2026 NPT refcon, we reaffirm our obligations and seek stronger verifications and transparency. As a part of the nuclear weapon free zone in Central Asia, Kyrgyzstan will continue to promote cooperation between such zones. The International Day for Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Awareness is a key platform for raising global awareness, youth engagement and education, promoting dialogue and cooperation, and supporting international commitments. A side event dedicated to this international day was held in March of this year, organized jointly by Cornell Repp Institute, the Kyrgyz mission, and the UN Office for Disarmament Affairs. Experts and panelists discussed how to inspire and educate students about disarmament, especially in the regions with limited access of such education. Mr. President, As artificial intelligence develops, it is crucial to closely monitor its potential impact on international stability. This includes military use of AI, autonomous weapons, and cybersecurity risk, and this information. As my president mentioned during the Security Council open debate, Kyrgyzstan believes AI must serve peace, conflict prevention and the protection of human life. We call for international rules on the responsible use of AI. All countries, not only developed ones, must benefit from these technologies. We also stress the need to prevent an arms race in outer space. Space must be used only for peaceful purposes. Weaponizing space threatens global security. Let us choose cooperation over confrontation, Let space remain a shared frontier of peace. Kyrgyzstan supports trust, solidarity, and cooperation in global affairs. We aim to build a multilateral system that fits today's changing world. And I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Kyrgyzstan for his statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Jordan.

Mr. Chair, allow me to begin by congratulating you on assuming the chairmanship of the first committee in the current 80th session of the General Assembly. We wish you every success. My country's delegation looks forward to closely working with your chairmanship to achieve the goals that we have set out. Mr. Chair, my country's delegation aligns itself with the statement made by the Arab group and NAM. We wish to make the following remarks in our national capacity. We reiterate the importance of international concerted efforts to peacefully settle conflicts, including a durable end to the war against the Gaza Strip. We welcome the signing of the agreement on Gaza today in Sharm El-Sheikh, and we commend the decisive role undertaken taken by the US president to reach this agreement, to commit to the end of war and to advance peace in the region. We underline the importance of honoring the ceasefire in Gaza, the implementation of all of its provisions to end the war and to remedy the disastrous consequences of the aggression against the Gaza Strip, as well as to allow the delivery of adequate and immediate humanitarian assistance to end the famine caused by the wanton aggression against the Gaza Strip. As for our topic of discussion today, we reiterate our steadfast position. in support of advancing nuclear disarmament and an honoring of our agreed commitments, including to achieve the universality of the NPT, to address current mounting international tension. We call for the honoring of these commitments within a defined timeframe to pave the way for total elimination of nuclear weapons. without supplanting this with interim measures that do not respond to the needs of non-nuclear weapon states. We warn against the integration of AI in the administration of nuclear weapons. We stress the need to ensure human control over these weapons to pave the way for their total elimination. We look forward to the success of the NPT Review Conference to be held next year. and the adoption of a comprehensive and balanced outcome document that focuses on the implementation of agreed commitments, especially the elimination of nuclear weapons, the universality of the Treaty and the establishment of a nuclear weapons-free zone in the Middle East. We call for full implementation of the 1995 Conference resolution on the establishment of this zone. We urge member states to support the outcomes of the various sessions of the conference on the establishment of the WMD and nuclear weapons free zone in the Middle East. We call upon all countries to support efforts made in the region to ward off the threat of unconventional weapons against it. as this jeopardizes international and regional peace and security. Based on the aforementioned, we once again renew our call to Israel to partake in the conference without preconditions and to accede to the Non-Proliferation Treaty and place its nuclear facilities under the comprehensive safeguards of the IAEA. Mr. Chair, Jordan underlines the need for outer space to remain limited to peaceful uses. We call for a legally binding instrument to prohibit non-peaceful uses and we welcome resolution 512/79. We also welcome the achievements made in the framework of the open-ended working group on the prevention of an arms race in outer space. As for cybersecurity, we support international efforts to ensure ICT security. We welcome the final report of the open-ended cybersecurity working group last July, and we express our full appreciation to its chair, permanent representative of Singapore, and we welcome the reports findings on the need to establish a global platform to address this vital file under the auspices of the United Nations. We look forward to the beginning of its work through the coming organizational meeting to be held in the coming month of March. As for conventional weapons, we stress the need to implement the United Nations Program of Action on Small Arms and light weapons to ensure non-acquisition of such weapons by terrorist groups. We call on the strengthening of the support provided to developing states to foster their border security. We welcome the outcomes of the preparatory meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Global Framework on Ammunition held in New York. in June, as well as the outcome document adopted by consensus, in addition to the template for national voluntary reporting and the priority matrix. And we look forward to the Conference of the Parties to be held in 2027. We stress the need to ensure that this global framework does not overlap with other mechanisms, namely the Programme of Action on Small Arms and light weapons. There is a need to ensure complementarity between all those mechanisms at the same time. We stress our full support to the deliberation of the first committee and we look forward to cooperating with Member States during the current session. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Jordan and I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of the State of Palestine.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Allow me, Adal Sid, to congratulate you and the members of the Bureau on assuming the chair of the First Committee this session. The State of Palestine places full confidence in your stewardship and reaffirms its commitment to supporting the successful work of this Committee. The State of Palestine associates itself with the statements of Arab Group and Non-Aligned Movement. Mr. Chair, the State of Palestine reiterates that only adherence to the Charter of the United Nations and to international law remains the indispensable foundation of international peace and security. The position use or threat of use of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction under any circumstances continues to constitutes a grave breach of the fundamental principles of international law. We reaffirm that the only durable remedy to the threat posed by nuclear weapons is their complete and verifiable elimination. Nuclear weapons states and nuclear-armed states bear a special responsibility for our collective security and must take concrete, time-bound and transparent steps toward dismantling their arsenals rather than expanding or modernizing them. Mr. Chair, While weapons of mass destruction pose existential threats to humanity, the immediate and catastrophic humanitarian toll of conventional weapons, especially when used in populated areas, demands urgent attention. Explosive weapons in all its forms have been shown to cause the vast majority of civilian casualties. Their effects and the systematic damage they inflict on innocent civilians and civilian infrastructure is catastrophic. A genocide can be committed by using conventional weapons when employed in unconventional manners. In Gaza, the consequences of sustained use of explosives in densely populated areas have been devastating. Extremely high civilian casualty figures, widespread injury and trauma, the destruction of vital civilian infrastructure and mass internal displacement. These are the horrifying consequences to the intensive use of explosive weapons by the Israeli war machine. When such conventional weapons are employed indiscriminately or in disregard of international law, their effects become mass scale in both scope and severity. In human terms, they function as weapons of mass destruction. We are further alarmed by the humanitarian and legal implications of integrating advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, into military surveillance, targeting, and strike systems, especially when rigorous human review and control are not guaranteed. As we have witnessed the horror of its use in Gaza, AI-assisted systems, including autonomous weapons systems, can accelerate targeting cycles. generate expansive target lists, and heighten the risk of misidentification and disproportionate harm to civilians. We underscore that meaningful human control must be preserved over the use of force at all times, and that any employment of AI in military domain must be governed by strict legal, ethical, and operational safeguards with transparent accountability. In this vein, we support the negotiation of a legally binding instrument on autonomous weapons systems that prohibits systems that cannot be subject to meaningful human control and all systems designed to target persons and establishes positive obligations and regulations on all other systems to ensure effective human judgment, predictability and accountability. Mr. Chair, the Middle East zone free of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction is a priority of profound regional and global significance. The United Nations Conference mandated by General Assembly decision 73/546 has already convened five sessions, adopting rules of procedure, establishing working committee and modalities, and issuing outcome reports that reflect constructive engagement. We look forward to the sixth session in next November under the presidency of the Kingdom of Morocco, and we commend the progress achieved thus far in consolidating this conference in an inclusive and consensus-based platform. Yet, despite these important steps, the conference cannot fulfill its mandate as long as the only nuclear-armed state in the region continues to remain outside the process. has not acceded to the NPT and refuses to place its nuclear facilities under full scope of IAEA safeguards. This persistent refusal defies repeated UN resolutions, including the 1995 resolution on the Middle East, and prevents the realization of the zone, which is an integral part of the package deal that enabled the indefinite extension of the NPT. Universal participation is therefore indispensable. The State of Palestine continues to engage in good faith so that the Conference can agree on a legally binding treaty. We call upon the international community to provide sustained support to this process and to urge the only non-participant to join without delay, so that the Middle East may finally be freed from the threat of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction for the benefit of present and future generations. Mr. Chair, with respect to outer space, the State of Palestine stresses the necessity of preserving the exclusively peaceful use of this domain. Preventing an armed race in outer space must be treated as a priority. We support multilateral negotiations toward a legally binding treaty that prohibits military activities, protects civilians and scientific assets, establishes norms of responsible behavior. Mr. Chair, we believe that security built on armament is fleeting. Lasting security is built on law, justice, development, and cooperation, and I thank you.

Thank you, the distinguished representative of the State of Palestine for his statement. Before giving the floor to the next speaker, I would like to consult the committee on its program of work. Members would recall that the general debate is expected to conclude on Friday 17 October in the afternoon. Given the progress made so far in terms of exhausting the list of speakers for the debate, and I do thank delegations for respecting the time limit, the Bureau would like to propose that the Committee begin listening to statements under the nuclear weapons cluster in the thematic discussions on Friday 17 October should the need arise. This change to the programme of work is without prejudice to the schedule of panels and briefings set out in document A/C.1/80/CRP/2. The Committee will also continue to devote at least half a meeting 90 minutes on 17 October in the afternoon to hear statements by representatives of civil society in an informal setting as agreed at the committee's organisational meeting. If I hear no objection, may I take that the committee wishes to proceed accordingly? I hear none. It is so decided. The committee will now continue its general debate. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belarus.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Congratulations on your election to this very responsible post. You can count on the support of the Republic of Belarus. Today, the world stands at a crossroads. The current anniversary session of the UN General Assembly marks the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II, a tragedy which claimed tens of millions of lives, leaving destroyed cities and mutilated lives in its wake, a war that changed the fate of humanity. Years have gone by and history is once again putting us to a tough test. on which the fate of our entire planet depends without exaggeration. The global crisis besetting the world order determines the international agenda. The architecture of international security underpinned by bilateral and multilateral mechanisms, non-proliferation and arms control continues to deteriorate. Conflicts are prompting an increase in military spending and provoking an escalation of the arms race. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, SIPRI, in 2024, military spending increased by 9.4%. That's equivalent to 2.7 trillion US dollars, a record not seen since the 1980s. The destructive conflict on Europe's borders rages on. We are located on the cusp of this bloody confrontation, and we, more than anyone else, see the corrosive consequences of this conflict. Against this backdrop, we're seeing active militarization on the European continent. We see ongoing tensions in the Middle East. From time to time, we see volatile hotspots emerging in South Asia, in Africa, and in other regions as well. New weapons, new kinds of weapons are emerging, which could change the strategic balance of power. Given that states don't have reliable security guarantees, nor genuine confidence building measures, the role of nuclear deterrence is on the rise. Belarus stands convinced an arms race in the 21st century is madness, something humanity cannot afford. Thus, we'd like to reiterate our full commitment to multilateral efforts to strengthen global security and our undertakings on non-proliferation, disarmament, and arms control. We believe that the NPT is a key component of the nuclear non-proliferation regime on which the entire system of international security hinges. We're disquieted by the fact that the third session of the NPT Review Conference PrepCom which was held in the spring of this year did not manage to adopt substantive outcome recommendations. This attests to the fact that there are ongoing divergences of principle between nuclear and non-nuclear states, which will have an impact on the overall unfavourable state of affairs in the run-up to the NPT review conference scheduled for next year. We call on all states to exhibit political resolve and to do their utmost to find points of convergence with a view to ensuring that the RevCom scheduled for 2026 to ensure that it makes a tangible contribution to strengthening the nuclear non-proliferation regime. We remain convinced that an inextricable component of these efforts are measures to develop an universal agreement on non-nuclear weapon states safeguards, as well as safeguards against the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons. We're in favor of mobilizing international efforts so as to ensure the immediate entry into force of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty. We call on states who haven't yet done so to immediately set in motion domestic procedures to accede to the CTBT. Belarus continues to actively cooperate with the IAEA on peaceful nuclear power. We are committed to our undertakings as regards nuclear security at the highest level. Mr. Chairman, what is equally dangerous is what's happening in cyberspace. Cyber threats are on the rise, as is manipulation of information, the use of digital technologies to exert political pressure and to interfere in the internal affairs of other states. All of this requires urgent international regulation. We welcome the outcome of the 11th substantive session of the OEWG on security of and in the use of ICTs held in July, as well as the unanimous adoption of the session's final report. We stand ready to actively contribute to the work of the future permanent open-ended mechanism on ICT security. The parameters thereof were determined by the OEWG session. A number of countries are withdrawing from the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention. This serves to weaken this important disarmament and humanitarian mechanism. What it also does is further destroys the security system on the European continent. The Chemical Weapons Convention remains one of the key disarmament and non-proliferation instruments at our disposal. We call for the OPCW to be depoliticized, for its activities to return to consensus with a view to restoring the effectiveness of the convention regime. We support efforts to strengthen the Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention, we're in favor of legally binding norms for verifying compliance with the convention's provisions. We're concerned by reports about the fact that in some countries there are projects underway to establish large-scale biotechnological centers, including in very close proximity to Belarus. Such sites are usually highly closed and as a rule of thumb, their range of functions is unclear and opaque. We call on countries involved in the establishment of such centers to exhibit greater transparency as per their undertakings under the BWC. We believe that Security Council Resolution 1540 is a singular instrument allowing us to adopt a comprehensive approach to combating the proliferation of WMDs and related materials. We stand ready to continue sharing our experience of cooperation on how to fulfill the full potential of resolution 1540 at the national and regional levels. We attach particular importance to the prevention of an arms race in outer space. We support the initiative on no first placement of weapons in outer space, as well as other initiatives aimed at strengthening confidence and transparency in this sphere. Belarus stands ready to engage in constructive cooperation with all UN member states at the First Committee with the view to de-escalating tensions, strengthening peace, security and stability. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Belarus and I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Philippines.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. My delegation congratulates you on your assumption as Chair of the First Committee. We are confident that under your leadership we will navigate the complex issues before us. The Philippines aligns itself with the statements delivered by Malaysia on behalf of ASEAN and by Uganda on behalf of NAM. Mr. Chair, we meet at a time when multilateralism is under strain yet never more essential. The trust deficit among states demands that this committee remain a forum for principled engagement and collective resolve. The Philippines reaffirms its constitutional and moral commitment to the international nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime. The NPT remains an indispensable foundation. We congratulate Ambassador Do Hung Viet of Vietnam on his designation as President of the 2026 NPT Review Conference and look forward to working closely with him toward a successful outcome. Progress on the implementation of the NPT has long been at a standstill. We urge renewed dialogue and meaningful action, especially on the practical steps under Article VI toward verifiable, irreversible disarmament, and for nuclear weapons states to accelerate the implementation of their obligations under the 64-point action plan. We likewise call on states to join the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which reinforces the humanitarian principles underlying the NPT. As a member of the IAEA Board of Governors, the Philippines stresses that peaceful uses of nuclear energy must not be treated as secondary to disarmament and non-proliferation. The recent passage of our National Nuclear Energy Safety Act underlines our commitment to this advocacy. Access to nuclear science, technology and innovation remains an inalienable right of all states parties to be pursued safely, securely and sustainably for development and human welfare. CTBT's entry into force remains one of the clearest, most attainable measures to contain nuclear escalation. Yet, entry into force is blocked by outstanding ratifications among the annexed two states. The Philippines urges those states to undertake the political decisions required to remove this obstacle and to refrain from conduct that would undermine the global testing taboo. As co-president of the 2025 to 2027 Article 14 process alongside Sweden, the Philippines remains committed to universalizing the CTBT and strengthening its verification regime. We also reiterate the long-standing call for the immediate commencement of negotiations on a fissile material cut-off treaty. Such a treaty is an essential and long overdue confidence-building measure. The Conference on Disarmament must be resourced and politically supported to resume meaningful work on this treaty without preconditions. Our delegation regrets the continued paralysis, but this should not diminish our determination. Instead, it should compel renewed political courage. Mr. Chair, the evolving character of conflict demands that we expand our legal and norm building efforts to emerging technologies. Cyber operations, artificial intelligence in the military domain, and lethal autonomous weapons system pose systemic risk to civilians and global stability. We urge all state parties to develop binding measures to ensure that military applications of AI remain consistent with international law, especially international humanitarian law. The recently concluded open-ended working group on security of and in the use of ICTs has started the path toward a permanent global mechanism. The Philippines supports its prompt operationalization and resourcing to ensure inclusive participation of developing states. On lethal autonomous weapons, we continue to support the Convention on Conventional Weapons Group of governmental experts and encourage it to pursue measures that uphold international humanitarian law and human responsibility for use of force decisions. We join like-minded states in urging the development of a concrete, universally applicable and legally binding instrument to govern lethal autonomous weapons system. We must not forget the human dimensions of conventional weapons, the cross-border and transnational threats of small arms and light weapons and their illicit trade fuel conflict, organized crime and human suffering. We welcome progress under the global framework for through life conventional ammunition management, including the 2025 preparatory meeting that advanced practical cooperation on safety and accountability. The Philippines has further demonstrated dedication to global disarmament through the recent enactment of our Chemical Weapons Prohibition Act, which bans the development, production, stockpiling, and use of chemical weapons in fulfillment of our CWC obligations. We continue to advocate for stronger legal frameworks for chemical weapons and other weapons of mass destruction. We affirm our support for both the norms, rules and principles of responsible behavior for reducing space threats and a legally binding instrument on the prevention of an arms race in outer space to maintain outer space as a peaceful and cooperative environment. Regionally, the Southeast Asia Nuclear Weapons Free Zone exemplifies cooperative risk reduction. We welcome recent movement toward broader protocol adherence by nuclear weapon states, which would buttress regional stability. The Philippines will continue to pursue practical measures that lock in non-use and protect our people from the specter of nuclear harm. The Philippine champions the participation of civil society, youth, women, consistent with the women peace and security agenda to ensure that our deliberations reflect the diversity of most affected by conflict. At the recent IAEA General Conference, the Philippines, as penholder on behalf of the G77 and China, helped secure a consensus resolution on staffing and women in the IAEA Secretariat, guiding human resource development in the nuclear field worldwide, especially for developing countries and women. Mr. Chair, our appeals are not abstract. We propose concrete, verifiable steps. Together, these measures will reduce risk and restore credibility to multilateral arms control. We further call on the parties to the New START Treaty to extend it or conclude a successor agreement before its 2026 expiration, preserving verifiable limits on strategic nuclear arms. Mr. Chair, the Philippines stands ready to work constructively with all partners to offer capacity building, to support verification friendly language, and to champion human security as a central objective of disarmament. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
Distinguished representative of Philippines for her statement. I give now the floor to his Excellency, Permanent Representative of Timor-Leste.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. We congratulate you on your assumption of the chair of the first committee. Timor-Leste aligns itself with the statement delivered by the non-aligned movement and wish to offer the following remarks in our national capacity. Mr. Chair, Timor-Leste reiterates its unwavering support for the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, which serves as a cornerstone of disarmament and non-proliferation architecture. We welcome the Secretary-General's recent report which encourages renewed momentum toward the universalization of its goals, especially in light of the increasing nuclear risks and technological developments in 2025. We call on the eight remaining Annex II states whose ratification is required for the treaty's entry into force to do so without delay. The continued existence of nuclear weapons is an unacceptable threat to humanity. It undermines global security, diverts resources from development, and contravenes the principles enshrined in the UN Charter. We therefore urge all nuclear weapon states to fulfill their Article 6 obligations under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, NPT, and to heed the 1996 International Court of Justice advisory opinion, which affirmed the illegality of the threat or use of nuclear weapons and underscored the legal obligation to pursue and conclude negotiations leading to nuclear disarmament. Timor-Leste supports the development of a legally binding instrument on negative security assurance to guarantee that non-nuclear weapon states will not be subject to the threat or use of nuclear weapons. Such a measure would strengthen confidence in the NPT, reduce asymmetries in the security landscape and advance the cause of a world free of nuclear weapons. Mr. Chair, Timor-Leste welcomes the ongoing process to establish a Middle East zone free of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction. Establishing such a zone would not only contribute to regional security, but also reinforce the global non-proliferation regime. More broadly, Timor-Leste recognises the crucial role of regional and sub-regional confidence-building measures. These include transparency in military expenditures, prior notifications of military exercises, and conventional arms control measures. Such steps foster mutual trust, reduce misperceptions, and prevent escalations of the situation. Mr. Chair, in our region, Timor-Leste reaffirms its strong support for the Treaty on the Southeast Asia Nuclear Weapon-Free Zone, CNWFZ. As a candidate for ASEAN membership, Timor-Leste is committed to fully upholding the principles of the treaty and contributing to a region free of nuclear weapons. We urge nuclear weapons states to sign and ratify the protocol of the Southeast Asian Nuclear Weapon Free Zone without reservations, which would strengthen the treaty's integrity and enhance regional peace and stability. The treaty serves as a successful example of how regional cooperation can advance global disarmament objectives. Mr. Chair, Timor-Leste welcomes the continued operation and further development of the United Nations Register of Conventional Arms and encourages all member states to provide greater support and greater reporting to enhance transparency in arms transfers. Transparency is not an end in itself. It is a critical measure for building confidence, preventing diversion, and reducing the risk of destabilizing accumulations. We also commend the strong cooperation between the United Nations and the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. The Chemical Weapons Convention remains a landmark in multilateral arms control. Its implementation must be strengthened, including through accountability for violations and universalization of the convention. No state should be outside this norm. Mr. Chair, Timor-Leste remains gravely concerned about illicit trade in small arms and light weapons. which continues to fuel armed conflict, destabilize communities, and impede sustainable development. While these weapons are small in size, their impact is devastating. Timor-Leste has taken concrete measures to address this challenge, including the adoption of national legislation, implementation of community-based disarmament initiatives, and close cooperation with regional partners to curb illicit trafficking. However, international efforts alone are insufficient. National efforts alone are insufficient.
