We therefore recommend enhanced international assistance for capacity building, especially in developing states, full implementation of the Programme of Action on Small Arms and Light Weapons and the International Tracing Instrument, including improved data collection and reporting, stronger integration of armed controls with sustainable development goal 16, recognizing that peace, justice, and strong institutions are mutually reinforcing with disarmament objectives. Mr. Chair, the rapid evolution of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, autonomous weapons systems, cyber capabilities, and space technologies presents both opportunities and risks. Timor-Leste supports efforts to ensure that such technologies are developed and used in strict conformity with international humanitarian law, ethics standards, and multilateral oversight. We welcome the work of the open-ended working group on ICT security and encourage inclusive, transparent, and gender-sensitive participation in these discussions. The military applications of AI, if left unregulated, could lower the threshold for conflict, increase the speed of escalation, and undermine human accountability. Therefore, Timor-Leste calls for greater transparency and reporting on military AI programs. Second, the development of norms and guidelines to ensure human control and accountability in the use of autonomous systems. And third, inclusive international dialogue to ensure that developing countries can meaningfully contribute to norm setting in this evolving domain. Mr. Chair, verification and transparency remain at the heart of effective disarmament. Timor-Leste supports the work of the Group of Scientific and Technical Experts on Nuclear Disarmament Verification, whose efforts contribute to the development of robust and credible mechanisms that build confidence and ensure compliance. Mr. Chair, Timor-Leste strongly condemns any attempts by non-state actors to acquire or use weapons of mass destruction. We call for strengthened international cooperation to prevent terrorism-related proliferation, including through through full implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1514, enhanced border and export controls, and targeted capacity support for states with limited resources. Finally, Timor-Leste reaffirms its support for the follow-up to the 2013 High-Level Meeting on Nuclear Disarmament, and we welcome ongoing efforts to revitalize the Conference on Disarmament and the broader disarmament machinery. Timor-Leste stands ready to work with all member states to advance disarmament, uphold international peace and security, and ensure that future generations inherit a safer, fairer, and more peaceful world. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Sir Walter for his statement. We now go to the distinguished representative of Turkey.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. At the outset, I wish to extend my sincere congratulations to you and esteemed members of the Bureau on your election. You can count on my delegation's full support. Mr. Chair, we are in a period of persistent political instability. Challenges around us have placed considerable strain also on effective multilateralism and disarmament architecture. This year we commemorate the 80th anniversary of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. As such, it is also a sobering period to remember the need to preserve the integrity and relevance of established disarmament and non-proliferation regimes. Mr. Chair, the wars in Ukraine and Gaza challenge the very principles we seek to uphold, protection of civilians, peaceful resolution of disputes, and the ultimate pursuit of a world free of weapons of mass destruction. After years of intense conflict with immense humanitarian consequences, the war in Ukraine continues to have profound global implications for international peace and security, while adversely affecting European security. Hence, we must persist in seeking a peaceful and negotiated settlement to the conflict. Our unwavering commitment to diplomacy is guided by the principles of international law, the UN charter, and the imperative of ensuring Ukraine's sovereignty, security, and territorial integrity. Turkey will continue with its diplomatic efforts to that end. We welcome the ceasefire in Gaza announced on October 9 and the efforts of the United States, Egypt, and Qatar. Ceasefire should be fully implemented. Humanitarian aid should go into Gaza without any restriction. Recovery and reconstruction should be launched right away. A lasting peace in the Middle East can be achieved only through a just settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. We hope that the momentum achieved in the ceasefire negotiations will also contribute to the realization of a two-state solution in the coming period. Mr. Chair, Turkey remains committed to the ultimate goal of a world without nuclear weapons and to ensuring safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear energy. Yet this process demands realism, sustained engagement, and the active participation of nuclear weapons states. The path towards a world without nuclear weapons is not easy, and even with the strongest political will of all states, could take years to achieve. In the meantime, reducing nuclear risks is critical. This is not an alternative to efforts towards nuclear disarmament, but to ensure that nuclear weapons will never again be used even while they exist. We remain committed to the NPT and its full implementation across all three mutually reinforcing pillars, disarmament, non-proliferation and peaceful uses. The upcoming 2026 NPT Review Conference provides another important opportunity to advance the treaty's objectives. Turkey remains committed to contributing constructively to efforts towards and during the review conference for a successful transition towards the subsequent review cycle, upholding the treaty's integrity and credibility, as well as maintaining the momentum on its universalization. Turkey regards the CTBT as another cornerstone of the global nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation architecture. We reiterate the importance of its universalization and urge the remaining Annex II States to take the necessary steps towards its entry into force and for all countries to uphold the moratorium against nuclear testing. As we approach the special 30th anniversary, it is worthy calling the motto, one treaty, one goal, zero tests. As the expired date of the New START is approaching, we welcome recent political statements for continuation of adherence to numerical limits and remain supportive of efforts and engagement for a follow-on arrangement. Recent situation in the Middle East, including the de facto recognition of nuclear weapons possession by a non-NPT state, also reaffirms the urgency of pursuing a Middle East zone free of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction, as envisioned in the 1995 Review Conference and the 2010 Action Plan. The international community must amplify efforts alongside all willing regional partners to advance this longstanding goal. Mr. Chair, despite the current situation with the JCPOA, Turkey continues to believe that concerns related to Iran's nuclear program should be settled through dialogue and diplomacy. We reiterate the need for all relevant parties to engage in negotiations for reaching a follow-on arrangement and remain supportive of efforts in that regard. At the same time, it also remains essential that the IAEA will continue to fully exercise its monitoring and verification activities in accordance with its mandate, and that its credibility and professionalism be upheld. We also reiterate our serious concerns regarding the continued development of the nuclear and ballistic missile programs of the DPRK. We firmly support the goal of complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula. In this context, we call for the resumption of meaningful dialogue and negotiations among the relevant parties. Mr. Chair, after years of obstruction by the former Syrian regime, the political situation since 8 December has opened a window of opportunity for the OPCW to establish a more effective working relationship in Syria. This new dynamic provides a basis to address longstanding issues related to Syria's chemical weapons programme and to advance sustained compliance with the CWC. We welcome the ongoing cooperation and engagement between the Syrian authorities and the OPCW. We also take note of the concept plan prepared by the Syrian authorities for the destruction and verification of any remaining chemical weapons. Mr. Chair, Turkey place high priority on strengthening international cooperation in the realm of conventional weapons. We reaffirm our unwavering commitment to the comprehensive implementation of the United Nations program of action on small arms and light weapons alongside the international tracing instrument. We regard the arms trade treaty as a key instrument for fostering responsible arms transfer and enhancing transparency. Turkey is a member of all export control regimes and maintains a robust and comprehensive export control system. Turkey remains firmly committed to counterterrorism and to advancing international cooperation in this domain. We urge all stakeholders to take concrete measures to prevent the diversion of arms to terrorist entities, which undermines regional and global security. The evolving applications of emerging technologies, particularly lethal autonomous weapon systems powered by artificial intelligence, remain a matter of strategic importance. Turkey is committed to ensuring that ethical safeguards, meaningful human control, and full compliance with international law and norms guide all AI-related developments, including the military domain. We also reaffirm our support for advancing norms of responsible state behavior in outer space and for strengthening transparency and confidence building measures in this increasingly vital domain. The escalating scale and sophistication of cyber threats underscore the urgent need for collective action and responsible state behavior in the digital domain. The continued proliferation of WMD and their delivery systems pose a serious threat to international peace and security. Of particular concern is the risk of such weapons and the materials used in their manufacture falling into the hands of terrorist groups and organizations. Turkey attaches high importance to collective efforts aimed at reversing this alarming trend and reinforcing the global non-proliferation regime. Mr. Chair, before concluding, let me also recall the Pact for the Future, which we welcome as a landmark initiative that also reaffirms the centrality of disarmament, non-proliferation, and arms control in the UN's vision for global peace and security. We stand ready to contribute constructively to the work of the UN First Committee. Thank you, Mr. Chair.

Mr

Chairman, Excellency Maurizio Massari, Permanent Representative of Italy, at the outset I would like to congratulate you on your election to steer the proceedings of the first committee during this session. We hope that this will be an opportunity to restart the political process so as to establish an independent Palestinian state with 1967 borders and East Jerusalem as its capital, so as to guarantee justice, security and stability throughout the region. We welcome the outcome report and the voluntary national reporting template. Next, we welcome the adoption of the final report of the in July 2025 and the mechanism so that at the United Nations we can continue to build states capacity, capacity to tackle the use of these means for criminal purposes. I thank the distinguished representative of Mauritania for his statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Hungary.

Thank you, Mr Chair. Let me join previous speakers in congratulating you upon your election and assure you of my delegation's full support. Hungary associates itself with the statement delivered and to be delivered by the EU in all clusters. However, in relation to Russia's war aggression against Ukraine, Hungary has more reservations compared to other EU member states. Mr. Chair, global security is increasingly challenged by persistent conflicts, terrorists, the erosion of arms control agreements, the spread of weapons of mass destruction, and the misuse of emerging technologies. In this complex security environment, the risk of escalation and miscalculation has never been higher. No state can address these threats alone. Hungary firmly believes that the objective of arms control, disarmament and non-proliferation is more important than ever. Hungary attaches great importance to the full implementation and universality of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which is the cornerstone of the global non-proliferation architecture and nuclear disarmament. We support concrete progress under Article 6 towards the ultimate goal of a world free of nuclear weapons and look forward to the 11th Review Conference to be held next year in New York. Hungary remains committed to the entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty and calls on all states, particularly the remaining Annex II states, to ratify the treaty without delay. It is regrettable that after more than three decades, the CTBT is still without entry into force. Hungary is deeply concerned about the nuclear and ballistic missile programmes of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, which pose serious threats to regional and global security. We urge the DPRK to comply with all relevant UN Security Council resolutions and to abandon its nuclear weapons in a complete, verifiable and irreversible manner. Hungary is also concerned about Iran's nuclear activities and emphasizes the importance of full compliance with its obligations under the NPT and its safeguards agreement. The International Atomic Energy Agency's independent verification role remains indispensable and Hungary will continue to contribute actively to its work. Mr. Chair, Regarding nuclear disarmament, Hungary shares the ultimate objective of achieving a world free of nuclear weapons. In light of the growing threat of nuclear weapon use, it is imperative that we intensify our efforts to defend and reject policies that threaten with their use. At the same time, it is important to recognise that there is no shortcut to nuclear disarmament. It requires an incremental approach that can yield tangible results. Our focus should be on identifying those areas where common ground and consensus that includes nuclear weapons states can be reached. We must actively explore avenues for achieving significant progress in strategic nuclear risk reduction, transparency and confidence building, as well as in working out robust verification measures. We also continue to support negotiation on a verifiable Fissile Missile Cutoff Treaty, the FMCT. Regarding existing and newly emerging risk, Hungary recognizes the growing impact of emerging technologies on international peace and security. We support decisions on the responsible military use of artificial intelligence and remain committed to advancing work within the Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems. Hungary reaffirms its unwavering support for the Biological Weapons Convention and the Chemical Weapons Convention. The use of chemical or biological agents under any circumstances is unacceptable and must not go unpunished. Hungary supports efforts to strengthen the BWC, including through the ongoing work of its working group, and highlights importance of the OPCW in ensuring full accountability for violations of the chemical weapon ban. Hungary attaches great importance to conventional arms control and disarmament instruments. We emphasize supporting the Mine Ban Convention, the CCW and the new global framework on ammunition management. We stress the need to prevent the diversion and illicit trafficking of small arms and light weapons, which continue to fuel conflicts around the world. Hungary also stresses the importance of preventing an arms race in outer space. We support the universalization of the Outer Space Treaty, the development of responsible norms of behavior, and the strengthening of the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs. We are content that the open-ended working group on PAROS was able to start its work this July. We strongly support international efforts to effectively prevent the weaponization of space and believe that outer space must remain a domain free of conflict. In cyberspace, Hungary supports the UN framework for responsible state behavior and advocates for confidence-building measures, capacity building and the strengthening of global cyber resilience. Mr. Chair, Hungary stands ready to work with all partners to advance peace, security and disarmament. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Hungary for her statement. I give now the floor to His Excellency, Ambassador of Switzerland for Disarmament and Multilateral Affairs.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to congratulate you on your election to the chair of our committee. We assure you of our delegation's full support. Mr. Chairman, Switzerland welcomes the 20-point plan of the United States of America, whose aim was to put an end to the war in Gaza. Any initiative must be rooted in international law and lay the foundations for a lasting peace in the Middle East based on the two-state solution. The release today of the 20 living hostages, the ceasefire in place and the delivery of humanitarian aid to the people of Gaza are crucial stages of the first phase of the plan's implementation. Switzerland calls upon all parties to honour their commitments. Mr Chairman, developments in the field of international security in recent years are a source of grave concern. The policies of might is right is on the rise and that poses many challenges to multilateralism. The world has become less stable, increasingly unpredictable and more and more divided. As such, military arsenals, including nuclear arsenals, are also growing. A certain number of international norms are being called into question, namely through open violations of the UN Charter. We've seen violations of the prohibition of the use of force or and in attempts to undermine the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states. Key international instruments have been violated, international humanitarian law has been violated. We're seeing increasing recourse to weapons viewed as running counter to international humanitarian law by the majority of states. Global economic competition is going hand in hand with arms races that we're seeing on the battlefield. I have talked about difficulties in terms of upholding international law and difficulties in export control regimes but these are more necessary than ever before we cannot lose sight of goals in this area and the importance protecting civilians from the effects of hostilities fostering de-escalation and building trust between states making progress towards general and complete disarmament under effective control and strengthening IHL as a whole a world governed by force and not by law imperils peace, security and prosperity in all corners of the globe. As such, the global rules-based international order and the international order based on consensus-based arms agreements negotiated decades ago must be upheld and promoted. International instruments in this area must be supplemented where that proves necessary. In this connection, I wish to underscore three crucial points. Firstly, The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons is the cornerstone of disarmament and nuclear non-proliferation regimes. It is also a central instrument in terms of global stability. The upcoming review conference in 2026 must produce positive outcomes. We call upon all states parties to collectively work towards that goal. My second point is that we must focus on the risks and challenges linked to emerging technologies and provide responses to them, namely by establishing new norms when necessary and by preparing the ground for future frameworks and new instruments whenever possible. My third point, we must preserve progress made in terms of humanitarian disarmament, progress made in the last 30 years. Renewed efforts must be made to promote norms established in this regard. Finally, we need to build trust, increase transparency, foster dialogue and encourage constructive discussion between states in order to abate risks and avoid misunderstandings. Mr Chairman, the crisis affecting the multilateral system coincides with an important juncture for the United Nations, namely the celebrations of its 80th anniversary. Against that backdrop, my delegation is closely following the UN 80 process, namely regarding the peace and security thread thereof. The savings plan proposed by the United Nations here points to the fact there are resource deficiencies, so there needs to be structural reform. And the structural reform within UNAT must be carefully done and managed in an ordered fashion. We must preserve multilateralism, preserve what works, and ensure that the UN is able to hold substantive technical debates. This UNAT process gives us an opportunity to assess the functioning of disarmament mechanisms established by the first emergency special session of the United Nations General Assembly devoted to disarmament. Such an assessment has been postponed for too long and we need to seize the opportunity to make this disarmament regime evolve if necessary. We underscore the unique added value that Geneva provides as a global centre of disarmament diplomacy and in terms of arms control. There we have the expertise of the diplomatic community, relevant organisations and everyone else combined. The UN in Geneva hosts many disarmament organisations and many legal technical experts. There is a strong presence of the disarmament office in Geneva and that is essential to ensure the effective running of the UN peace and security architecture. Switzerland is ready to constructively work to ensure that UN 80 allows us to equip the UN with the means necessary to address today's and tomorrow's challenges. Mr Chairman, in a world characterised by the riding tide of risk, and the erosion of norms, Switzerland remains determined to promote human sharing values and defend the rule of law. We must strengthen multilateralism and ensure the United Nations preserves the tools and the trust it requires to preserve peace and security for generations to come. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
Thank you to the distinguished representative of Switzerland for his statement. Again, I'll go to the floor to His Excellency, Permanent Representative of Moldova.

Mr. Chairman, let me begin by congratulating you and the members of the Bureau on your election. You can count on the full support of my delegation for a successful and forward-looking session. We continue confronting destabilizing hybrid operations with cyber attacks, disinformation, and foreign information manipulation, interference designed to undermine our democracy, artificially create ambiguity among population, and derail our European path. And just in the same line, we also join other speakers who previously expressed concern over China's insufficient transparency with regard to its nuclear policy. In this regard, we welcome the Gaza peace plan presented last week by President Trump and note to satisfaction the first steps to implement that they have already taken place. We stand ready to support this process and call on all actors in the region to play a constructive role in fostering stability and peace. We urge Iran to fulfill an open and constructive cooperation with IAEA, as recorded in the September 9, 2025 agreement signed in Cairo. Chair, to conclude, Romania remains committed to promoting and strengthening multilateral instruments in the field of arms control, disarmament, and non-proliferation. And I think.
I thank the distinguished representative of Romania for her statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Croatia.

Mr. Chair, Croatia's path to sovereignty has been shaped by our commitment to peace, freedom and democratic values. From our non-aligned position during the Cold War, through the experience of armed aggression in the 1990s, into EU and NATO membership. Croatia has consistently demonstrated dedication to collective and cooperative security. Guided by these principles, Croatia remains concerned by the grave humanitarian situation in Gaza. We commend President Trump's leadership in bringing about a negotiated agreement and commend all efforts aimed at de-escalation and alleviating civilian suffering. It is essential to ensure full unimpeded humanitarian access, uphold international humanitarian law, and secure the safe release of hostages. Croatia expresses hope that these steps will pave the way for a new dialogue and lasting peace. At the same time, Croatia unequivocally condemns the Russian Federation's unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression against Ukraine. and firmly supports its independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity. We actively contribute to efforts aimed at safeguarding nuclear safety and ensuring accountability for violations of international law. We remain a strong advocate of multilateralism and rules-based international order. Arms control, disarmament, and non-proliferation are not ideals, but instruments of peace and security. Our own experience when facing aggression without deterrence has taught us the cost of insecurity and the value of solidarity. In this context, nuclear deterrence within NATO's collective defense posture remains a key to strategic stability and peace. It is defensive, proportionate, and consistent with the UN Charter and international law, providing credible security assurances to non-nuclear allies to reduce proliferation incentives. Croatia calls on all nuclear weapons states to recommit to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. Ahead of the 2026 review conference, we urge transparency, accountability, and a meaningful outcome. We support the early entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty and regret the Russian Federation's deratification. Remaining Annex II states should sign and ratify the treaty without delay. Additionally, we support prompt negotiations on a fissile material cut-off treaty and a global moratorium on fissile material production for nuclear weapons pending its adoption. Strategic stability requires transparent nuclear doctrines. We urge all nuclear-armed states to align policies with verifiable actions, enhance transparency about their arsenals, and engage in meaningful risk reduction. We particularly encourage China to increase transparency regarding its nuclear doctrine and arsenal and to take tangible steps to reduce strategic risks. Mutual trust must rest on openness and dialogue. We remain deeply concerned by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea's continued nuclear and missile development in violation of the United Nations Security Resolutions and urge its return to full compliance with its international obligations and dialogue toward denuclearization. Croatia reconfirms the importance of the New START Treaty and supports expanding strategic arms control frameworks. We urge all nuclear-armed states to engage constructively in nuclear arms control negotiations, which are essential for global security. We strongly support arms trade treaty, which promotes transparency and responsibility in the global arms trade, and emphasize the full implementation of the ATT to prevent diversion and strengthen expert controls, especially for dual-use goods and technologies. Russia commends the International Atomic Energy Agency's role in ensuring nuclear energy use for peaceful purposes and supports its full, timely, and transparent cooperation with Iran. Full access and compliance are critical for regional stability and the integrity of the non-proliferation regime. We welcome the renewed cooperation of the new Syrian authorities with the Organization on the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons and encourage further engagement to verify the complete elimination of chemical weapons. Constructive participation is vital for restoring trust and upholding Chemical Weapons Convention. Korea reiterates its firm support for both the CWC and Biological and Toxins Weapons Convention. The use or threat of use of chemical or biological weapons is unacceptable. In this regard, we underscore the importance of safeguarding the independence and credibility of mechanisms such as OPCW and the UN Secretary-General's mechanism. As a country once heavily affected by landmines, Croatia remains committed to the full implementation of the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention and continues to support demining, particularly in Ukraine, through technical expertise and humanitarian aid. Solidarity in demining is an investment in lasting peace. Krishan underscores the persistent threat of small arms and light weapons and supports full implementation of the UN Programme of Action and the Global Framework for Through-Life Conventional Ammunition Management. Strengthened controls, stockpile security and expert monitoring are key to preventing conflict and enhancing human security. Regarding emerging technologies, creation emphasizes that legal autonomous weapon systems must comply with international humanitarian law, ethical standards, and democratic values. We also recognize that both outer space and cyberspace, while offering immense potential, also pose serious security challenges. Responsible behavior must extend beyond Earth and into cyberspace. We support the application of international law to space activities and welcome the work of the UNOWG on the prevention of an arms race in outer space, as well as UN framework for responsible state behavior in cyberspace and the new global mechanism on ICTs to advance transparency, capacity building, and accountability. Strengthening responsible conduct and resilience in this domain is essential to safeguarding international peace and security. Mr. Chair, Croatia remains a constructive partner in advancing peace, security, and disarmament. Guided by our national experience, anchored in international law, and our strategic alliances, we will continue to support diplomacy, responsibility, and multilateral cooperation to address the challenges of today and tomorrow. I thank you.
Thank you, the distinguished representative of Croatia, for her statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Slovenia.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Let me join others in congratulating you and the members of the Bureau upon your appointments. Slovenia will be engaging constructively throughout the session. We align ourselves with the statement delivered by the European Union and wish to make the following additional remarks in our national capacity. Mr. Chairman, we meet at a time of profound uncertainty. Conflicts are intensifying, trust among states is strained, arms control and disarmament frameworks are eroding, while new technologies are reshaping the world. What can the international community do, as well as what can this organization do? For Slovenia, the answer is clear. Respect and uphold international law and bring more certainty into an uncertain world. I wish to begin this year's intervention by focusing on regional security issues. We condemn Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine, which continues to cause immense human suffering and destabilise the wider region. Slovenia stands with Ukraine, its right to self-defence, and with international efforts towards an unconditional ceasefire and a comprehensive, just and lasting peace. We call on Russia to respect the UN Charter and international law and to end its war in Ukraine immediately. We welcome the comprehensive plan to end the war in Gaza. and the beginning of the ceasefire, offering an opportunity for a lasting peace. Wars, even when IHL is respected, brings death, destruction and suffering that transcends a single generation. When the law is ignored or deliberately violated, accountability must be ensured. Impunity cannot be tolerated. This is true for the war in Ukraine, in Gaza and all other conflicts around the world. Slovenia will continue working with the partners to both alleviate the humanitarian crisis and to pursue negotiated solutions to conflicts. This includes supporting a deal that would prevent Iran from acquiring the nuclear weapons in return for lifting nuclear-related sanctions. Slovenia wishes to see the regime and objectives of the JCPOA meaningfully restored. There is no other but diplomatic solution to the challenge of Iran's nuclear program. Mr. Chairman, turning to the NPT, Slovenia will work towards a successful outcome of the 2026 review conference. The NPT remains the cornerstone of nuclear disarmament, non-proliferation architecture, and the peaceful uses of nuclear energy. Article six awaits its full implementation. Slovenia calls on nuclear weapons states to meet their disarmament obligations, enhance transparency and risk reduction measures, and re-engage in a substantive arms control dialogue. NPT is much more than a legal instrument. It represents an understanding between generations, a promise to prevent the nuclear flames of war, to advance the peaceful atom, and to keep alive the hope of the world free of nuclear weapons. A comprehensive ban on nuclear tests is an essential step toward that world. Slovenia urges all states, especially those whose ratification is required, to sign and ratify the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. Mr. Chairman, let me turn to the issue of technology. The rapid development of artificial intelligence in the military domain makes ongoing discussion on lethal autonomous weapon systems increasingly urgent. AI brings threats as well as opportunities in maintaining peace and security, as we have recently discussed in the Security Council. Slovenia acknowledges the limited but meaningful progress achieved in the Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems, as well as the work undertaken through initiatives such as the RE-AIM process. While we recognize the potential of AI technologies, it is vital to remember that behind every algorithm, there still stands a human. This underscores the central principle of human responsibility and accountability, which must guide both our multilateral efforts and national approaches. On a related note, Slovenia welcomes the successful conclusion of the open-ended working group on security and use of information and communication technologies. We look forward to continuing discussion on development in the field of ICT in the context of international security and advancing responsible state behavior in the use of ICTs within the new global mechanism. Mr. Chairman, Slovenia remains fully committed to the Ottawa Convention, including through its engagement in the convention's machinery, such as Committee on Enhancement of Cooperation and Assistance in the 26-27 period. Slovenia will continue to work towards a mine-free world, including through ITF Enhancing Human Security, a humanitarian organization which continues to help communities worldwide to overcome deadly legacy of mines. Before concluding, I wish to reiterate Slovenia's commitment to a multilateral system based on international law, in particular the UN Charter. We also wish to emphasize the obligations stemming from binding international treaties, In this context, and being aware of the importance of the Chemical Weapons Convention and its universality, Slovenia has decided to run for the seat in the Executive Council of the OPCW for the period of 2026 to 2028. We are determined to contribute to the effective work of the Organization, prevent further proliferation of chemical weapons and their use, and contribute to the destruction of all remaining stocks of re-emerged chemical weapons. I wish to conclude, Mr. Chairman, by highlighting the importance of gender dimension in arms control, disarmament and non-proliferation. Slovenia firmly believes that the meaningful participation of women in these processes contributes to more effective, inclusive and sustainable outcomes. We will share additional views on specific issues in our cluster statements. I thank you, Mr. Chairman.
I thank the distinguished representative of Slovenia for her statement. I give now the floor to the distinguished representative of Gabon.

This proliferation and modernization also fuels fear of global destabilization and unspeakable humanitarian disasters. In a world that is destabilized, in a world of conflict and manifold crisis, and given the challenges posed by new technologies such as AI and autonomous weapons system, it is more urgent than ever before to renew our collective commitment to disarmament, non-proliferation and international security. In view of the aggressive rhetoric of a number of States rooted in the possession of nuclear weapons, we must succeed in their immediate, complete, irreversible and verifiable elimination. In this connection, my delegation reaffirms the importance of international instruments in the field. Specifically, the Non-Proliferation Treaty, which is the cornerstone of the disarmament regime, and the CTBT. we must achieve the universalization of the NPT and in that vein my delegation calls upon all stakeholders to engage in candid comprehensive dialogue to guarantee a successful outcome for the 11th NPT review conference to be held in 2026 this is vital in order to guarantee consensus on a comprehensive outcome document moreover we encourage the international communities to support other treaties such as the TPNW. We call for the extension of such nuclear weapons free zone to other regions of the globe in order to bring about a safer world. We also hail the crucial role played by the IAEA. Another major challenge is that of the irresponsible trade in small arms and light weapons. The proliferation of these continues to fuel conflicts, terrorism and organised crime. And these phenomena have particularly devastating effects on civilians, namely on women and children. We must step up international cooperation by ensuring stringent implementation of tracing and marking mechanisms. We must also ensure that manufacturers and exporters shoulder their responsibilities in this regard if we are to effectively thwart illicit trafficking in these weapons and contribute to increasing the peace and security of our people. The time has come to do just that, Chair. Protecting outer space has also become an imperative for our collective security. Space is essential for communication, navigation and crisis management. As such, it must not become a new arena for military confrontation. The establishment of legally binding norms and rules will allow us to prevent an arms race in space and to guarantee that it can be used peacefully for the benefit of us all. In the face of the aforementioned threats, capacity building remains a prerequisite for developing countries to effectively contribute to global disarmament and non-proliferation efforts. This involves specialized training programs, the creation of modern surveillance infrastructure and increased access to knowledge transfer. Chair, cooperation, dialogue and diplomacy must prevail over confrontation and mistrust. Sustainable peace is a matter of shared responsibility and to achieve it, each and every one of us must be resolute and committed. There is an urgent need to reduce herculean military expenditure and to instead funnel these resources into global priorities, combating climate change, responding to health crises, preventing humanitarian disasters and achieving sustainable development goals. I thank you.

Thank the distinguished representative of Israel for his intervention, and I call now the representative of the USA to take the floor.

Thank you, Chair. I would like to respond to several inaccurate and misleading statements during the general debate regarding US extended deterrence, defense spending and force modernization, and conventional weapons deployments. The United States has long worked to advance global non-proliferation objectives and prevent additional states from acquiring nuclear weapons. In the face of growing threats, U.S. extended deterrence arrangements have successfully reassured allies that they can remain secure without acquiring nuclear weapons of their own and contributed to the preservation of regional stability and the prevention of nuclear war, core goals we all share. The strategic nuclear forces of the NATO alliance, and particularly those of the United States, are the supreme guarantee of NATO's security. NATO's nuclear burden sharing arrangements have always been fully consistent with the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, including throughout its indefinite extension. The United States maintains full custody and control of its nuclear weapons wherever they are in full conformity with Articles I and II. While we consult with our allies about matters of security and defense, No NATO allies or otherwise ever have control over U.S. nuclear weapons. Our further extended deterrence consultation mechanisms with the Republic of Korea, Japan, and Australia are a critical pillar in a broader strategy designed to preserve peace, deter conflict, and ensure a free and open Indo-Pacific. Chair, it is concrete measures like these and others, such as ballistic missile launch notifications and the use of secure communication centers that build the confidence and trust that is so lacking in the current environment and demonstrate my country's commitment to a safer world. Thank you, Chair.
